introduction: The guide opens with a plain rule of reading: the Holy Books have their own terminologies, and when scripture says that Zion is dancing it means that her people rejoice. From there these readings interpret one figure after another, the sun and moon of prophecy, the wolf and the lamb, the heavenly Jerusalem, the reed, the cloud, the seed, the bread from heaven, and then use figures of their own: mirror, cage, tree, garden, sword in its sheath. Here they are read beside the texts they interpret, given as those texts stand, the Gospel’s darkened sun, Isaiah’s peaceable kingdom, the Qur’an’s Verse of Light and its Throne, and beside others who have thought about how figures work: Paul on letter and spirit, Emerson on the roots of words, Plato’s cave, Blake’s grain of sand. Some of the company resists. The Qur’an warns against those who pursue the allegorical, Paul stakes faith on an event, Milton tells the Fall as history, and Wordsworth’s Peter Bell sees a primrose and nothing more. The question they raise together is the guide’s own: how is a figure read truly, and what keeps the reading from being whatever a reader pleases?
questions: The first readings say that scripture must be read by its own terminology. What do Paul’s “the letter killeth” and the Qur’an’s warning about the allegorical verses each add to that rule, and where do they pull apart?

Several readings interpret a passage that is given here in its own words: the darkened sun, the wolf and the lamb, “no more sea”, the Throne. Choose one. What does the interpretation keep of the passage, and what does it set aside?
The miracles, one reading says, “were spiritual teachings, not literal”. Hume and Paul both object, from opposite sides. What is each defending, and how might the readings answer them?
Everything on earth, a reading says, is a symbol of heavenly things. How do Blake’s grain of sand, Emerson’s account of words and Wordsworth’s primrose bear on that claim?
The body appears in these readings as a cloud, a cage and a veil; Paul calls it a temple and Lovelace denies that bars make a cage. What difference do these figures make to how a person lives?

When a figure is explained, as heaven, the cross, paradise and the Trinity are explained here, is anything lost? Consider Milton’s Satan on the mind, Paul on the stumbling-block and Xenophanes on the gods of oxen.

outside.why: “In the scripture we read that Zion is dancing. It is evident that this has other than literal interpretation.” Isaiah has mountains that sing and trees that clap their hands, and no reader has taken him for a naturalist: it is how the joy of a returning people is said.

The Holy Books, says the reading, “have their special terminologies which must be known and understood”. Paul states the stake in a phrase that became a rule of reading: the letter kills, and the spirit gives life.

By “sun”, “moon” and “stars”, the reading says, are meant the laws and teachings of a Dispensation; a later reading takes the “cloud” as the human body. This is the passage of the Gospel being read: sun darkened, stars falling, and the Son of man coming in the clouds.

The reading interprets the sun, moon and stars of prophecy with confidence. The Qur’an divides its own verses into clear ones and allegorical ones, warns against those who pursue the allegorical to cause dissension, and reserves the explanation to God. Who may say what a figure means, and by what warrant?

To speak of the spirit “you are obliged to describe them in terms of sensible things”, as when grief makes the heart “heavy”. Emerson finds the same law in the dictionary: every word for a moral or intellectual fact was borrowed from something seen, and spirit first meant wind.
The reading takes the leopard and the kid, the lion and the calf, as hostile peoples brought to fellowship. This is the verse it is reading, from Isaiah’s picture of the peaceable kingdom.

By the holy Jerusalem “descending out of heaven from God”, says the reading, is meant the Law of God. John’s vision is given here as he wrote it: a city coming down adorned as a bride, and a voice saying that God will dwell with men.

“When Christ speaks of water, He is symbolizing that which is the cause of Everlasting Life.” At the well in Samaria the two waters stand side by side, the one that leaves a person thirsty and the one that becomes a spring within.

The couplet says that a hidden hand guides the pen and a hidden rider the horse. FitzGerald’s Omar also sees only the writing and not the writer, and what he feels is that no line of it can be cancelled. Is the veiled hand in the reading a comfort or a fate?

The reading explains a reed that is emptied of its pith and so gives out melodies that are the player’s, not its own. The reed is the one that opens Rūmī’s Mathnawī, complaining of its separation from the reed-bed.

The body, says the reading, is a cloud that keeps a person “from beholding the Sun of Truth”. Paul describes the same hindered sight with a mirror in place of a cloud: now through a glass, darkly, and then face to face.
“Whatever there is on the earth is a symbol of heavenly things.” Blake asks for the eye that can read so: a world in a grain of sand, a heaven in a wild flower.

The reading makes the outer world a set of symbols for the spiritual one, the lamp for guidance and the seasons for the ages of religion. Paul had argued that the invisible things of God are understood “by the things that are made”.

For the reading every earthly thing stands for something heavenly. Wordsworth’s Peter Bell is the man for whom it does not: a primrose is a yellow primrose and nothing more. Is Peter missing something that is there, or declining to add something that is not?

The reading follows a teacher who found the name of the Báb foretold in the count of letters. The best-known such puzzle in scripture is here: the number of a name, offered to whoever has understanding.
The reading explains “the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea” as the passing of a former religion’s outward forms. This is the verse.
“Christ was like a seed, and this seed sacrificed its form so that the tree might grow.” The figure is his own, spoken of his death: the grain that falls into the ground and dies bears much fruit.
The reading takes Adam as spirit and Eve as self and says the verses have “numerous meanings”. Paul read Genesis in the same manner, and said so: Abraham’s two sons by two mothers “are an allegory”.

The reading turns Adam, Eve and the tree into the spirit, the self and the material world. Milton begins his epic with the story as an event, one man’s disobedience that brought death into the world. What is gained by reading it as the reading does, and what would Milton say is lost?

Asked what it means to eat the living bread, the reading answers: “the heavenly sustenance of divine perfections”. In the same chapter of John, when the hearers take offence at the saying, Jesus gives the rule for it: the flesh profits nothing, and his words are spirit.
“The splitting of the moon has multiple meanings and is not limited to its outward meaning.” This is the verse of the Qur’an in question, in a chapter named for it.

The reading makes the sea of Tiberias the ocean of creation and the boat the reasonings by which people gain knowledge. In Matthew’s telling a disciple leaves that boat on a word, and sinks when he looks at the wind.

The Sun of Reality rises from different points of the horizon, the reading says, and nations cling to the point and not the sun. A hymn of the Rig Veda says the like of names: sages give many titles to what is One.
“Jesus spoke everything in parables because the ideal sense is, in this way, revealed and understood.” The disciples asked him why, and here is the question with part of his answer.

The reading holds that parables reveal the meaning. The answer Jesus gives in the Gospel leans on this passage of Isaiah, where the message is sent so that people hear and do not understand. Does a figure open a meaning to everyone, or only to those ready for it?
“We can put the light of the lamp in another chimney and it is still the same light.” Rūmī says it in nearly the same image: the lamps are different, the Light is one.

The reading warns against becoming “attached to the chimney”, the personality, and forgetting the light. In John’s Gospel the light and the person are not to be separated: “I am the way”, and no one comes to the Father otherwise. How far can the lamp be distinguished from its glass?

“As long as man lives within the shell of the egg he cannot soar heavenward.” Plato’s figure for the same confinement is a cave, whose prisoners have been chained since childhood and see only what is in front of them.

Outwardly alone, says the reading, “in reality, invisible hosts of the Supreme Concourse are our aid”. Elisha’s servant saw only the besieging army until his eyes were opened on a mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.

“The sword He carried was the sword of His tongue, with which He divided the good from the evil.” The Letter to the Hebrews has the same reading of the sword: the word of God, sharper than any two-edged blade, dividing soul and spirit.

“The miracles of Christ were spiritual teachings, not literal.” Hume also declined to take the reports literally, for a different reason: no testimony can establish a miracle unless its falsehood would be the greater marvel. What does a reader who takes the miracles as teachings keep that Hume gives up?

The reading takes the miracles as teachings and not as events. Paul rests everything on one of them having happened: if Christ be not risen, preaching and faith are vain. Which is in more danger, a faith that needs the event or one that does not?

The reading considers a candle that can be sheltered only while wax and wick remain. Macbeth, hearing that his wife is dead, uses the same figure for a life and finds nothing behind it. The reading’s candle belongs to an argument; Macbeth’s to despair.
The reading crowds sun, stars and moons into a description of days of rapture. The psalmist had heard the same sky as speech: day utters it to day, without words, to the end of the world.
“Consider man as a sword: while it remains in its sheath, its quality remains hidden.” Tennyson’s Ulysses fears exactly that: “to rust unburnish’d, not to shine in use”.
The sword must leave the sheath, the reading says, for “the quality of man lies in his conduct and deeds”. The Gospel says it with a candle that is not lit to be put under a bushel.
Many shade trees are green and fruitless, the reading warns, but under the Tree of Life one “will certainly partake of fruit”. The Gospel gives the same test for telling one tree from another.
“The intent of ‘heaven’ is not this boundless space.” Asked when the kingdom would come, Jesus gave an answer of the same kind: not with observation, not here or there, but within.

The reading moves heaven from the sky to “the world of reality”. Milton’s Satan moves it into the mind, which can make a heaven of hell; he says so on arriving in hell. If heaven is not a place, what keeps it from being whatever a mind decides?
The reading quotes it: “His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp, the lamp within a glass.” Here is the Verse of Light in Pickthall’s English.
“Though chicory appears outwardly bitter, inwardly it is most sweet.” Shakespeare’s duke says it of adversity, ugly as a toad and carrying a jewel.
When the true River flows “through a new temple and fresh garment”, the reading says, the old edifices are drowned. The Gospel’s figure for the same event is new wine, which bursts the old bottles.

God “cast those spiritual realities … into molds of forms such as houris, palaces, flowers, rivers”, the reading explains. The Qur’an introduces its rivers of water, milk, wine and honey with the word the reading relies on: “a similitude of the Garden”.

Nearness comes “through the baptism of water and fire revealed in the Gospels”, the water being knowledge and the fire the love of God. This is the saying of John the Baptist from which the pair is taken.

“All praise be to God Who hath established the Throne upon the water.” The phrase is from the Qur’an’s account of creation, where it stands beside the purpose of the whole: to try which of you is best in conduct.

The reading builds a cosmology of throne, water, air and letters. Genesis begins with the same elements held more simply: a deep, a Spirit moving on the face of the waters, and a word that makes light.

The prayer praises the Name by which “the trees of the garden of Thy Revelation have been clad with verdure” in this Springtime. The Song of Solomon has that spring, with its flowers and the voice of the turtle-dove.

When Christ said he came from heaven, the reading says, he “did not mean the blue firmament”, and the clouds are what hid him from men’s eyes. In Acts two men tell disciples who are staring at the sky that he will come “in like manner” as they saw him go. What would those disciples have made of the reading?
A blessed tree “casteth its shadow upon all regions”. The Gospel’s tree of that kind begins as the least of seeds, and the birds of the air lodge in its branches.
The reading’s tree shelters every region. The Great Law of the Haudenosaunee plants a Tree of Peace whose roots run to the four directions, so that any nation may trace one back to its shade.

“The mirror’s glory lies in the sun’s rays being reflected in it”, so long as no veil of self intervenes. Paul writes of an unveiled face that beholds the glory “as in a glass” and is changed into the image it reflects.
The sun passes through each sign in turn and only after a full circuit blazes again in Leo. The Preacher gives the rule in general: to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose.
“The bird of your soul would not be contained in the cage of the body.” Socrates, on the day of his death, describes the soul as viewing existence “through the bars of a prison”.

The reading pictures the body as a cage the glad soul would leave. Lovelace, writing from an actual prison, says that walls and bars make no cage for a mind that is free in its love. Is the cage the body, or something a soul may be rid of while still in it?
For the reading the body is a cage. Paul calls it a temple, the dwelling of the Holy Spirit and not the soul’s own to despise. What follows for the care of the body from each figure?

Of one who has died: “That drop found its way to the Most Great Ocean.” The Upanishad’s rivers reach the sea and no longer know themselves as this river or that; the reading’s drop arrives and its bird still sings.

The letter asks what consolation could be greater than that the bird has reached its nest and the breeze its garden. Donne consoles himself by the same confidence and turns it against death in person.

The stars of heaven, says the reading, are sometimes in auspicious and sometimes in inauspicious stations, unlike the stars of the love of God. Cassius dismisses the heavens altogether: the fault is not in our stars but in ourselves. What do both deny to astrology, and what does only the reading put in its place?

The reading speaks of stars “in the ascendant of the love of God” that shine in other heavens. Daniel promises that the wise, and those who turn many to righteousness, shall shine as the stars for ever.

When the vina began the piano fell silent, and the reading draws a lesson from it. Elijah on the mountain learned a like one: the Lord was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but after them a still small voice.
“There is a Garden of God. Human beings are trees growing therein. The Gardener is Our Father.” In John’s Gospel the plant is a vine, the Father is the husbandman, and the fruitful branch is pruned.

A flower is a flower “in a valley, in a garden, in a vase”, and religion’s laws and forms are clothes it may change. Juliet says of a name what the reading says of a setting: the rose would smell as sweet under any other.
“The Tree needs rain, and when the rain falls whether it is warm or cold it does not matter.” Hopkins, in a dry season of his own, asks for nothing else.
A tree that bore fruit once and is now dead “is no longer a tree. Today, it must manifest harvests.” The owner of the fig tree in the Gospel reasons the same way after three years of looking.
To illustrate the Trinity the reading takes the sun, its ray and the one who receives the light. The Council of Nicaea had reached for the same image at the centre of its creed: “Light of Light”.

The reading offers an image by which the Trinity can be understood. The Qur’an addresses the same doctrine with a command: “say not ‘Three’”. Does the reading’s illustration answer the Qur’an’s objection, or accept it?

“The Altar of Sacrifice is the living heart of man and not a few pieces of dead stones.” The psalmist had moved the altar in the same direction: the sacrifice God accepts is a broken and contrite heart.

A tree that does not send its root deep is broken by one strong wind, the reading says, and a later one calls the unsteadfast “rootless plants”. Jeremiah’s tree spreads its roots by the river and does not notice the drought.

The sun shines on every mine, the reading says, but only the capacity of the mine makes a diamond. Portia’s mercy falls like rain on whatever lies beneath and asks no fitness. Why do some receive more from what is given to all alike?

“I liken you to the pupil of the eye. You are black and it is black, yet it becomes the focus of light.” Blake’s black child can only say that his soul is white. What does it change to make blackness itself the place where light gathers?
“In the Torah and Gospel, the divine Kingdom is likened to a garden and vineyard.” Isaiah’s song of the vineyard is one such place, and it ends with the owner looking for justice and finding a cry.

The dove has warbled and the garden is adorned, the reading says, and the croaking of the crow has risen too. In the Gospel’s field wheat and tares come up together, and the owner lets both grow until harvest.
To a couple the reading says: “You are two birds of one nest … and two moths of one flame.” Genesis makes the figure a single body.

The reading’s figures for marriage all make the two one: one nest, one dwelling, one flame. Gibran asks for distance inside the union, as the pillars of a temple stand apart. What does each figure protect?
The heavenly Farmer clears, harrows, sows and plants, the reading says. Paul uses the same field to put human labourers in their place: one plants, another waters, and God gives the increase.
“Do you think that if all the people in the world should unite that they can stop the coming of the Spring! No, it must perforce come!” Shelley ends his ode on the same certainty, as a question.

For the reading spring cannot be prevented, and that is good news. Eliot’s speaker feels the same inevitability as cruelty, because it stirs what had settled. Who would wish the spring delayed, and why?

“Is there any child who, after being born into the world, desires to return to the womb?” Nicodemus asked whether a man could enter the womb a second time, and meant it as an impossibility. The reading uses the same impossibility to argue that no soul would wish to come back.

No one freed from the cage would want it again, the reading argues. Hamlet describes how the matter looks from inside: the dread of an undiscovered country makes us keep the ills we have. Why does the bird in the reading not share Hamlet’s fear?
“I will take thee through its imperial palaces”, the reading promises of the next world. In John’s Gospel the promise is of a house with many mansions and a place prepared.
The reading sees a Youth mount a steed of light while the pillars of all things shake. John saw heaven opened and a white horse, whose rider was called Faithful and True.

The Beauty mounts “the saddle of light, even as the Spirit mounted the mighty throne”. The Qur’an tells in one verse of a servant carried by night to the farthest place of worship, the journey later tradition gave a steed.
The reading addresses someone “standing in the land of symbols, at Horeb of the Command … Sinai”. Horeb is where Moses turned aside to see a bush that burned and was not consumed.

A flower placed upon the water “rests like a crown”; so the reading prefers manifestation to concealment. Gray thinks of the flower that blooms unseen and the gem the ocean hides, and mourns the village dead with them. Is what is never shown wasted?

The reading turns from physical houris to spiritual ones and to “the fruit of light”. Paul declines to picture the reward at all: eye has not seen it nor ear heard. When is an image of paradise a help, and when should it be given up?

“Not physical houris who possess naught but appetite”, says the reading. FitzGerald’s Omar asks for the physical things, bread, wine and a companion, and calls that paradise enough. What does each think the other has mistaken?
“His days were but as the days of roses.” Herrick’s rosebuds are the same measure of a short life; he draws from it advice for the living, where the reading speaks an epitaph.
“The dawn hath broken … and the Sun crieth out: ‘To Me, to Me, O peoples of the earth!’” Isaiah addresses the city the light has reached: arise, shine, for thy light is come.
The prayer swears “by Thy Fig … and by the Olive Tree”. The oath is the Qur’an’s, at the opening of a short chapter: by the fig and the olive, by Mount Sinai.

The reading summons a heavenly Maid to step from the court of eternity and be seen only by those with insight. In Proverbs Wisdom is a woman too, but she stands at the gates and in the high places and calls to everyone.

“Once again the dove of eternity hath descended … in this gloomy and disastrous age.” The first dove of scripture comes back to the ark in the evening with an olive leaf, and Noah knows the waters have gone down.

The reading defends a law “to prevent the wolves from destroying the lambs”, sanctioned by the Shepherd. In John’s Gospel the good shepherd meets the wolf by giving his own life, and it is the hireling who runs.

It is right, the reading says, to dash the poisoned cup from a man’s hand “even with extreme violence”. The Qur’an lays down that there is no compulsion in religion, since right direction is distinct from error. Where does protecting the flock end and compelling it begin?

The form of the cross “is to be found in everything—even in this piece of cloth”. Justin Martyr made the same observation to a Roman emperor: the sail, the plough and the workman’s tools all have this shape.

The reading finds the cross everywhere as “the symbol of spiritual sacrifice”. For Paul it was first of all an execution that no one could find fitting: a stumbling-block to some and foolishness to others. What is lost when the cross becomes a universal pattern?

The reading relates a dream of standing in the place of the Imam while a multitude gathers behind. Joseph’s dream in the Qur’an has the same shape, the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowing to him, and his father warns him to keep it to himself.
“He is established upon the throne” meant nothing by “throne”, the reading says, “except His knowledge and power”. This is the verse, one of those on which Muslim theologians divided.

The reading refuses to let God be “established upon” anything, since that would give Him a likeness. Xenophanes made the same refusal by a joke: if oxen and horses could paint, their gods would be oxen and horses. Why is some figure still needed, even by those who know it is one?
“The messenger of Joseph was the bearer of his garment”, and by its touch Jacob “was endowed with sight”. This is the verse of the Qur’an behind the reading.
“The ‘holy city’ is the City of Love.” Augustine built his largest book on the same definition: two cities, made by two loves.

But those in whose hearts is doubt pursue, forsooth, that which is allegorical seeking (to cause) dissension by seeking to explain it. None knoweth its explanation save Allah

quran-moon-rent.text: The hour drew nigh and the moon was rent in twain.

quran-similitude-of-the-garden.text: A similitude of the Garden which those who keep their duty (to Allah) are promised: Therein are rivers of water unpolluted, and rivers of milk whereof the flavour changeth not, and rivers of wine delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of clear-run honey

quran-throne-upon-the-water.text: And He it is Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days - and His Throne was upon the water - that He might try you, which of you is best in conduct

quran-say-not-three.text: So believe in Allah and His messengers, and say not "Three" - Cease! (it is) better for you! - Allah is only One Allah

quran-fig-and-olive.text: By the fig and the olive, By Mount Sinai, And by this land made safe

quran-night-journey.text: Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far distant place of worship the neighbourhood whereof We have blessed, that We might show him of Our tokens! Lo! He, only He, is the Hearer, the Seer.

quran-joseph-dream.text: When Joseph said unto his father: O my father! Lo! I saw in a dream eleven planets and the sun and the moon, I saw them prostrating themselves unto me.

quran-established-on-the-throne.text: The Beneficent One, Who is established on the Throne.

quran-joseph-shirt.text: Go with this shirt of mine and lay it on my father's face, he will become (again) a seer; and come to me with all your folk.

emerson-spirit-means-wind.text: Every word which is used to express a moral or intellectual fact, if traced to its root, is found to be borrowed from some material appearance. Right originally means straight; wrong means twisted. Spirit primarily means wind
emerson-spirit-means-wind.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

blake-grain-of-sand.text: To see a World in a Grain of Sand / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower / Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand / And Eternity in an hour
blake-grain-of-sand.author: William Blake

wordsworth-yellow-primrose.text: A primrose by a river's brim / A yellow primrose was to him, / And it was nothing more
wordsworth-yellow-primrose.author: William Wordsworth

milton-first-disobedience.text: Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit / Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste / Brought death into the World, and all our woe, / With loss of Eden, till one greater Man / Restore us, and regain the blissful seat, / Sing, Heavenly Muse
milton-first-disobedience.author: John Milton

milton-mind-its-own-place.text: The mind is its own place, and in itself / Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven
milton-mind-its-own-place.author: John Milton

hume-testimony-miracle.text: no Testimony is sufficient to establish a Miracle, unless the Testimony be of such a Kind, that its Falshood would be more miraculous, than the Fact, which it endeavours to establish
hume-testimony-miracle.author: David Hume

shelley-spring-far-behind.text: Be through my lips to unawakened earth / The trumpet of a prophecy! O, Wind, / If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?
shelley-spring-far-behind.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

gray-blush-unseen.text: Full many a gem of purest ray serene, / The dark unfathom'd caves of ocean bear: / Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, / And waste its sweetness on the desert air
gray-blush-unseen.author: Thomas Gray
gray-blush-unseen.work: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard

shakespeare-brief-candle.text: Out, out, brief candle! / Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player / That struts and frets his hour upon the stage / And then is heard no more: it is a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing
shakespeare-brief-candle.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-not-in-our-stars.text: Men at some time are masters of their fates: / The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings
shakespeare-not-in-our-stars.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-undiscovered-country.text: But that the dread of something after death, / The undiscover'd country from whose bourn / No traveller returns, puzzles the will / And makes us rather bear those ills we have / Than fly to others that we know not of
shakespeare-undiscovered-country.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

plato-cave.text: Behold! human beings living in an underground den, which has a mouth open towards the light and reaching all along the den; here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them, being prevented by the chains from turning round their heads
plato-cave.author: Plato

justin-form-of-the-cross.text: For consider all the things in the world, whether without this form they could be administered or have any community. For the sea is not traversed except that trophy which is called a sail abide safe in the ship; and the earth is not ploughed without it: diggers and mechanics do not their work, except with tools which have this shape
justin-form-of-the-cross.author: Justin Martyr

xenophanes-oxen-and-horses.text: if oxen and horses or lions had hands, and could paint with their hands, and produce works of art as men do, horses would paint the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen, and make their bodies in the image of their several kinds
xenophanes-oxen-and-horses.author: Xenophanes

nicene-light-of-light.text: and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father
nicene-light-of-light.author: First Council of Nicaea

plato-bars-of-a-prison.text: The lovers of knowledge are conscious that their souls, when philosophy receives them, are simply fastened and glued to their bodies: the soul is only able to view existence through the bars of a prison, and not in her own nature
plato-bars-of-a-prison.author: Plato
